Most meetings are lost in the first minute, and it is almost never about the content. Here is what I teach people who chair meetings. In the first sixty seconds, say three things, and only three. One: why we are here. Not the history. The reason, in one sentence. Two: the agenda. How many items, and in what order. And say the order out loud, because the order is a decision too. Three: what you want to have at the end. A decision, a date, a name. If you say those three things, everybody in the room knows where the meeting is going, and they will help you get there. Then, every time you change item, say it. Moving on to item two. Going back to the price. It sounds too simple. It is not. People cannot see your agenda in their heads. You have to tell them where you are.

I have sat in a lot of good meetings that failed after they ended. Everybody agreed, everybody was happy, and two weeks later nothing had happened. So now I close every meeting the same way, and it takes five minutes. I stop the discussion five minutes before the end, even when it is a good discussion. Then I sum up: what did we decide, in one sentence each. Then the action items, and here is the rule I never break. Every action item gets one owner and one date. Not the team. Not marketing. A name. And not soon, or next week. A date. If an item has two owners, it has no owner. And the last thing, before anybody leaves: when do we talk next? If that is not on the calendar before the call ends, it is not going to happen.
